counterexample: Step 0005's parenthetical asserts: "if L=NP then every problem in NP is NP-complete under logspace reductions." Explicit counterexample: take the empty language A = ∅ over Σ = {0,1}. (i) A ∈ NP: the TM that halts and rejects on every input decides A in linear time, so A ∈ P ⊆ NP; this holds unconditionally, in particular under the hypothesis L = NP. (ii) A is NOT NP-hard under many-one (logspace or polytime) reductions, and this too is unconditional. Witness the nonempty language B = {1} ∈ P ⊆ NP. Suppose f were any many-one reduction from B to A, i.e. for all x ∈ Σ*: x ∈ B ⇔ f(x) ∈ ∅. The right-hand side is false for every x (nothing is a member of ∅), so B would have to be empty. But 1 ∈ B. Contradiction. Hence no reduction f exists, B ≴ A, so A = ∅ is not NP-complete no matter what L, P, NP turn out to be. Trace with the concrete string x = 1: the reduction must satisfy 1 ∈ B (true) ⇔ f(1) ∈ ∅ (false) — false ≡ true, impossible. The mirror-image counterexample is A' = Σ* ∈ NP: with the same B = {1}, take x = 0; the reduction needs 0 ∈ B (false) ⇔ f(0) ∈ Σ* (true, since f(0) is a string over Σ), again impossible. So ∅ and Σ* are two explicit members of NP that are never NP-complete under many-one reductions; the universally quantified claim "every problem in NP" is false, and the correct statement needs the word "nontrivial" (every NP language other than ∅ and Σ*). Scope note, checked: DNF-SAT itself is nontrivial — the string "x" is in DNFSAT and the string "x ∧ ¬x" is a DNF string not in DNFSAT — so the specific claim of 0005 (if L = NP then DNF-SAT is NP-complete under logspace reductions) survives, as does the equivalence in 0007.
reasoning_summary: Step-by-step verification. 0001 is framing, no content. 0003: the claim DNF-SAT ∈ L is true (scan each term and check no variable occurs both positively and negatively; two pointers plus counters fit in O(log n) space), though the stated justification, "assigning variables to satisfy the first disjunct," is a defective recipe as literally written — on (x ∧ ¬x) ∨ y the first disjunct is unsatisfiable while the formula is satisfiable, so one must find the first CONSISTENT term. I did not stop here because the step's assertion is true and repairable in one clause, and its second half ("if it is NP-complete then L = NP") becomes correct once the paper's own logspace-reduction convention, made explicit in 0005/0007, is applied: L is closed under logspace many-one reductions, so an NP-complete-under-≤log language lying in L forces NP ⊆ L. (Under the default Karp/polytime convention that half would only yield P = NP; that is an imprecision, but it admits no concrete witness, so it is not the early-stop point for this arm.) 0005 is where I stop with certainty: its main clause is fine (if L = NP, then for A ∈ NP = L run the logspace decider and output a fixed yes-instance or fixed no-instance of DNF-SAT — a legal logspace reduction, using that DNF-SAT is nontrivial and in NP), but the parenthetical generalization "every problem in NP is NP-complete under logspace reductions" is flatly false: ∅ and Σ* are in NP and can never be many-one-hard, as witnessed above. This is the classic missing hypothesis in "if P = NP then every NONTRIVIAL language in P is NP-complete." For completeness I checked the remainder: 0007's equivalence (L = NP iff DNF-SAT is NP-complete under logspace reductions) is correct in both directions, and 0009 is correct that L ≠ NP is weaker than P ≠ NP (L = NP would give P ⊆ NP = L ⊆ P, hence P = NP, so P ≠ NP implies L ≠ NP) and, by 0007, is exactly equivalent to the desired conclusion and therefore the weakest sufficient hypothesis. So the load-bearing argument reaches a correct conclusion; the defect is a false universally quantified assertion asserted as part of step 0005.
